departures_from_gist.departure: Chat length and regime. The headline Sonnet chat is 60 logged messages totalling 21,687 bytes; the view peaked at about 16.2 KB against the gist's 64-128 KB. The final view.json and cview.json of the Sonnet and Haiku chats hold only level-0 lines: no merged line was ever shown to any turn or compaction. The design is inert below 128 KB, so this is a test of UniiChat's start-up phase, about 12% of the way to its first batch.
departures_from_gist.fix: Disclosed in the lede and limits, but the title and the 'what it cost' section read as a verdict. Add one sentence directly under the cost table: 'in this chat no merged line ever entered a view; uniichat was running in its start-up phase, where the view is close to the raw transcript.'

departures_from_gist.departure: Message shape. The script's 26 user messages are 42 to 1,123 bytes, mean 270; only 5 exceed 512 bytes. 48 of 60 logged messages (Sonnet chat) were 512 bytes or less and went into the view word for word with no model call. Only 4 tool calls and 4 results, the largest result 185 bytes. The gist is written for agent work where tool results are clipped at 30,000 characters and a line compresses them about 60 to 1. Here the view was about 70% of the raw log.
departures_from_gist.fix: The post says 'messages near 1 kb', which the data contradicts. Replace the limits bullet with: 'the script was short question-and-answer: 60 logged messages, 21.7 kb in all, user messages averaging 270 bytes, 4 tool calls. 48 of the 60 messages fit in 512 bytes and entered the view verbatim, so there was almost nothing to compress.' Also fix the 'not much to compress' paragraph, which blames the 512-byte line size instead of the script.

departures_from_gist.departure: Eager merges were 81% of the compaction bill and nothing read them. In the Sonnet arm 36 of 49 compaction sends were merges (up to node 0+32), producing 675,919 of the 834,302 Haiku output tokens; in the Haiku arm 43 of 53 sends and 768,474 of 859,289 tokens. This follows the gist ('a merge starts once both its halves are built'), but none of those lines was consumed inside the experiment. It is prepayment in a 26-message chat, and at the same time a steady-state cost (about one merge per message forever).
departures_from_gist.fix: Add to 'the compactor': 'of the 49 compaction sends in the sonnet chat, 13 were leaves and 36 were merges, and the merges were 81% of the compaction output tokens. the gist builds a merge as soon as both halves exist, so we did too, but in a chat this short no merged line was ever shown to a call. in a long chat the same merges are needed eventually: about one per message.'

unfair_to_gist: Title, lede and brief all assume the gist promises savings. It does not. Its claims are: constant context size, nothing lost, no manual compaction, 'nearly every token is read from the prompt cache', and one cost comparison only (batched merging about 4x cheaper than merging at every message, 21 vs 80 line-inputs). 'the cost did not [reproduce]' and 'the savings did not show up' attribute to it a claim against a continued session that it never makes. The post admits this in the last limits bullet; it has to be in the lede.

'where the money went / the write price': 'the gist notes that subscriptions mark at one hour; it does not follow that through to the economics.' This is a jab, and the post's own data undercut it: at 1.25x writes the Sonnet turn ratio is 1.33x against 1.45x at 2x (final report, bottom line). The write price is a small part of the gap and the baseline pays the same 2x. On a subscription nobody pays per token anyway. Delete the sentence and give both ratios.

Cache note 1 ('one changed line rewrites the whole view ... a batch costs the whole view once, not the tail') is presented as the gist saying something different. The gist says 'A batch rewrites the view once' and 'The cache misses after ... a batch'. For the batched design the finding agrees with him. What it does challenge is his description of the alternative ('a merge changes the view from the merged line on', 53 of 192 lines per message): on the real cache a merge-per-message design would rewrite the whole view each time, which makes his batching argument stronger, not weaker. Say that.

Cache note 2 says 'the gist does not mention the limit'. It does state the mechanism: 'looks back up to 20 blocks from a mark for an earlier one'. What it omits is the consequence for a turn that adds more than 20 blocks. Also, through the API he has spare marks to place every 20 blocks; in Claude Code none is free. Part harness limit, part open question.

Cache note 3 ('the cache is per model') is listed under things the gist does not say. The gist says 'The cache misses after ... a switch of model or account.' The real point is narrower: 'reads them from the turns' cache entry' cannot hold when turns run on Sonnet or Opus and compactions on Haiku.

'the wait before a turn ... median 23 to 63 s, worst 296 s' is set against the gist's 'the wait takes seconds' (the report's verdict: 'does not hold at xhigh'). The harness started leaf compactions only after the turn finished and fired the next message immediately, with three experiments sharing the account. That is a harness upper bound, not the design's latency. The per-send wall time (leaf median 19-24 s at xhigh) is the fair number to give him.

'the missing predecessor' is presented as a structural property and asked as question 9. It is the gist's stated rule ('a message's node starts once fewer than 8 lines before it are still unbuilt'; 'the view stops at the first unbuilt line') combined with the harness logging a whole turn before compacting. The 80% rate is the harness's worst case.

'there is not much to compress yet ... a 512-byte line is not much shorter than a 1 kb message' blames the line size. The cause is the script: 48 of 60 messages were already under 512 bytes and were copied in verbatim, as the gist specifies. With 30 KB tool results the same line is a 60:1 compression.

'the compactor ... per line it was not [cheap]' is fair and is the post's best finding, but it should say that thinking volume is whatever Claude Code's --effort xhigh produced on claude-haiku-5-5; the mapping to his setting is unverified.

'standing orders fade' is fair as a counter to the gist's 'a correction given in chat survives up the tree, so most of an AGENTS.md becomes unneeded', provided the corpus density and the verbatim-key grading are stated next to it. The post already notes the untested part (whether the agent still obeys) and that corrections survived 21 of 21; keep both.
over_or_under_claims: OVER: 'built ... to the letter' (title) and 'we implemented the current revision exactly' (lede). Five features not built, four listed deviations, eight bugs (one fix not re-verified), and a request that Claude Code wraps. Use 'as closely as claude code allows'.

OVER: 'everything mechanical in the gist reproduced.' The report's verdicts are 'partly' for: kind tags (Haiku 79 of 112), never answering the data (Sonnet baits), zoom before guessing (Sonnet and Opus never zoomed in 32 turns at the gist's limits), 98.6% / 96.2% cache share, 'from the merged line on', and constant context size (one batch, scaled only). The sawtooth, the 16-32 KB compaction view in steady state, 11 lines per level and the 21-vs-80 batching result were not tested at all. Say 'the parts we could exercise behaved as described'.
OVER: 'at every length we tested'. Two lengths, 26 messages and 42 at scaled limits, both before the first batch at the gist's limits. Say 'in the one short chat we ran'.
OVER: 'on a claude code subscription there is no choice' about 1-hour writes. Untested; the harness itself requested ttl 1h on the view mark (claude_cli.py blocks_of).

OVER: 'true at xhigh across 549 sends: no heads, no preambles, no tool calls.' The report says no heads or preambles in 549 sends at all efforts; no tool calls at xhigh in 288 (E1) + 216 (E3) sends; at default effort Haiku called zoom in 5 sends. Split the sentence.

OVER: 'nothing is lost: zoom recovers it, 61 of 61'. Regex-graded by the harness, not re-run by the reviewer, at most 64 messages deep, and at the gist's limits the models answered from the line without zooming because the view was nearly verbatim. Add 'regex-graded, at most 64 messages deep'.

OVER: break-even 'roughly message 215 ... message 400 or later'. An extrapolation with zero measured points beyond 42 messages, for one turn model. The report adds 'earlier for Opus, never for Haiku turns', which the post drops. Either label it 'model prediction' with its assumptions (script shape, Sonnet turns, CLI prices) or remove it; the site rule separates predictions from measurements.

OVER (by mixing): 'one compaction send averaged 11,326 output tokens (n=116)' is E1, Haiku arm. The next sentence's 834,302 tokens is E3, 49 sends, which is 17,027 per send (median 11,418, max 70,943 for node 0+32; 30,619 thinking tokens for a 508-byte line in one sampled row). A reader will divide and find the numbers disagree. Give both with their source, and give median and max.

OVER: closing line says 'the frozen numbers, the call ledger and the list of what was and was not recomputed' are in studies/. The study folder holds only summary.json and manifest.yaml, and the manifest says 'raw call rows are not published here'. Remove 'the call ledger'.

OVER (provenance): the fidelity table, the order-survival counts, the 21 of 21 corrections, the answer grades and the prefix-only 97.5% are 'taken as reported', not recomputed by the reviewer. The post does not mark them. One footnote: 'recomputed from raw rows except: ...'.
OVER: subtitle says 'one question for the author'; there are nine.

UNDER: the strongest and most general finding is hedged away with the rest. Compaction cost per message does not depend on chat length: about one leaf per long message and about one merge per message, forever. At xhigh that was a median of about 11,000 and a mean of about 17,000 Haiku output tokens per send, nearly all thinking. 'we never reached the regime' does not weaken this; it is the one number that carries to a long chat, and it is what decides any break-even. The post files it as reason one of four and then says the whole result may be a regime artifact.

UNDER: effort versus fit is a clean, significant result (76 of 79 at xhigh against 47 of 79 at default on the same nodes, p < 0.01) and directly useful to him. It sits in a subordinate clause. So does 'the ruler made no significant difference' (37/37 vs 34/37, p = 0.24), which is omitted and which he would want to know.
UNDER: the turn-only ratio at the gist's own write price (1.33x at 1.25x) is missing. Without it the reader cannot see how much of 1.45x is the subscription's doing.

HEDGE THAT LOSES THE FINDING: 'this is not evidence that the gist is wrong. it is evidence that the gist's savings do not appear in a short chat driven through claude code.' The second sentence repeats the unfair premise. Say what was found: 'in a 22 kb chat uniichat cannot save anything, and its turn calls cost 1.3 to 1.5 times a cached continued session; separately, each compaction at haiku xhigh cost 11,000 to 17,000 thinking tokens, which does not depend on chat length.'
questions_review:
Nine is too many for a first message; four of them he can answer by pointing at his own text, which costs credibility for the rest. Keep three or four.

Q1 (saving against what, from what length): half answered by the gist's first paragraph: 'A session fills up, gets compacted or dropped, and the next one starts from zero. Long sessions also rot.' The gist claims no saving against a cached continued session. Reword so it does not presuppose a savings claim. The 'from what length' half is good.

Q2 (what does a compaction cost you): the sharpest question; lead with it. Add the distribution (median, mean, max) and the leaf/merge split.

Q3 (is your accounting on the API at 1.25x): answered verbatim. 'The prompt cache charges about 0.1x for a prefix it has seen and 1.25x to write a new one' and 'On the API, entries live 5 minutes from their last read. Don't buy 1-hour entries (they cost 2x to write) ... Claude Code subscriptions mark with their own 1-hour lifetime.' Drop it. Ask instead whether he runs on API billing or a subscription, since that decides what 'cheap' means.

Q4 (98.6% and 96.2% of what): answered: 'turns read 98.6% of their prefix from the cache, compactions 96.2%', 'measured by replaying 3,000 messages against a model of Anthropic's cache'. The only open part is whether the model stores entries only at marks. Fold into Q5 or drop.

Q5 (marks around a batch): answered. 'One cache mark sits on the last whole block and one on the request's end'; 'A batch rewrites the view once'; 'The cache misses after ... a batch.' He accepts one full rewrite and keeps no interior mark. The live remnant: does his cache model charge a merge 'from the merged line on' (prefix-exact) when the real cache charged the whole view? That affects his 53-of-192 and 21-vs-80 figures, in his favour.

Q6 (more than 84 new lines in a turn): sharp and not answered by the gist. Keep. Note that on the API he has spare marks and in Claude Code we had none.

Q7 (same model for turns and compactions): he knows the fact ('The cache misses after ... a switch of model'), but the gist also says a Haiku compaction 'reads them from the turns' cache entry'. Legitimate as a one-line clarification: 'are your turns on haiku too?' Merge into the 'how do you run it' question.

Q8 (standing orders): sharp, because it tests a specific claim: 'A correction given in chat survives up the tree, so most of an AGENTS.md becomes unneeded.' Quote that line. Do not guess his answer for him; the gist already says the user's instructions follow the system prompt. Ask whether he has seen orders (as opposed to corrections) drop out, and whether the agent still obeys them.

Q9 (is the missing predecessor intended): answered. 'A message's node starts once fewer than 8 lines before it are still unbuilt' and 'A compaction's view stops at the first unbuilt line, so no call ever sees a placeholder or half a message.' It is the stated rule, and our 80% rate is partly our feeder. Drop, or ask only whether he tried a stricter gate.

Missing questions an expert would expect:
- How do you run it: API key or subscription, which turn model, which Haiku version, and does 'xhigh' on Haiku spend about 10,000 or more thinking tokens per line for you? (Decides whether our compaction number is his number.)
- In daily use, what share of your tokens or spend is compaction, and roughly how many compaction calls per message?
- What do your messages look like: what fraction are over 512 bytes, and how many messages before the first 128 KB batch? (Ours: 20% over 512 bytes, 22 KB after 26 user messages.)
- Merges are built as soon as both halves exist, about one per message, long before any view needs them. Is that deliberate (so a batch never blocks), and did you try building them lazily or at a lower effort than leaves? In our runs merges were 81% of compaction tokens and the highest ones cost most (70,943 tokens for 0+32).
- Is UniiChat expected to cost more than a plain cached session until the first batch? Is there a length below which you would not use it?
- Would a cheaper setting with more retries do? We measured first-try fit 96% at xhigh against 59% at default, and the ruler made no significant difference.
tone_and_title:
Tone is mostly respectful and plain, and the limits section is honest. Three things would put him off.

1. Title. 'we built uniichat to the letter. the mechanism works. the savings did not show up.' overstates three times: 'to the letter' (features not built, bugs, wrapped request), 'the savings' (the gist promises none against a continued session), 'did not show up' (in a 22 KB chat where the design is inert). To the author it reads as a debunk, and the body then walks it back. Suggested: 'uniichat through claude code: the mechanics hold, and compaction is the bill' with subtitle 'victor taelin's one-chat-that-never-ends, rebuilt from the october 11 gist and run on haiku, sonnet and opus. a short chat, 1,343 requests, and four questions for the author.'

2. Lede. Accurate about what the gist says in its first sentence; inaccurate in 'implemented ... exactly', 'the cost did not', and 'at every length'. It is right to say the regime was not reached, and that sentence should come before the cost claim, not after.

3. Two sentences read as point-scoring: 'it does not follow that through to the economics' and the framing 'things ... the gist does not say, or says differently' over items the gist does say (model switch, lookback, a batch rewrites once). Retitle that section 'cache behaviour we measured' and attribute each item correctly.

Form. About 2,300 words with seven tables; he will not read all of it unprompted. The questions are at the very bottom and half are answerable from his text. Put the three or four real questions in the note itself and near the top of the post (a short 'what we would ask' box after the lede). 'a second agent that had not written the code checked it' should say plainly that the build and the review were done by AI agents under the owner's direction; he will ask. Before sending: push the branch, pin the gist revision hash, and ideally add the round-two result, since the post says a 250-turn run at real limits 'is running now' and he may reasonably reply 'come back when that is done'. If the owner sends now, the note should say round two is coming and ask what he would want measured in it.
clarity: Cost table has no unit on the first two numeric columns and mixes two measures. Columns 2-4 are weighted token units for turn calls only; columns 5-6 are USD including compactions. The visible ratio (1.45x) is not the ratio of the USD columns (5.0x, 58x). Split into two tables or label: 'turn calls only, weighted tokens (input-token equivalents of the turn model)' and 'whole arm incl. compactions, usd (cli estimate)', each with its own ratio.

'cost unit: input + w x cache write + 0.1 x cache read + 5 x output' needs one more clause: these are relative API list-price weights, the unit is one uncached input token of the turn model, and on a subscription this is a notional cost.
'opus, 6 late questions' is undefined. Say: 'opus answered only the last 6 recall questions, on a chat seeded from the sonnet run, in both arms; none needed a compaction.'

'xhigh', 'effort', 'mark', 'block', 'lookback', 'ruler', 'the cut', 'leaf', 'batch', 'w' are used before they are defined. One short glossary line each for effort (the model's thinking-budget setting), mark (a cache breakpoint), and batch (the 128 to 64 kb merge) would cover it for a reader who has not seen the gist.

'three experiments' are never named. One line: 'E1: can models write the lines (80-message synthetic corpus). E2: cache behaviour with synthetic views. E3: a 26-message chat in both arms.' Then tag each table row or paragraph with its experiment, since E1 and E3 numbers are mixed in the compactor paragraph.
'what reproduces' table mixes synthetic and real: rows 2, 3 and 4 are E2 with synthetic view text, row 6 includes scaled-limit data. Add a source column (E1/E2/E3, synthetic or real, scaled or not).
'1,343 calls' are API requests reserved on the ledger (the report counts 1,244 call rows; 5 reservations have no row). Say 'requests'.
'the first-message formula matches at 481, the number the gist gives' is cryptic. Say: 'the wrong formula the gist warns against matches push at only 481 of 20,001 steps, as the gist says.'
'no free cache mark' in limits is not explained. Say: 'the api allows four cache marks per request and claude code uses all four, so we could not add one.'

'a thinned claude code session, 3,851 to 4,627 tokens of overhead, not a stock one at 28,793' should say what was removed (default tools, settings, plugins, MCP) and that a stock baseline would make the continued session dearer per call but also cached.
Latency paragraph: define 'the wait before a turn' as the time to build the previous turn's missing leaf lines, and state how it was measured (see the harness note in departures).
Fidelity table header 'after three merges (8 messages per line)' needs 'forced in a separate experiment; in the cost chat no merged line was shown'.
'our marks at the end of the view' should say whose design that is: the gist's ('one cache mark on the last whole block').
The earlier post is linked as 'optchat-long-horizon-v0.html' with the old name OptChat; say once that OptChat is the gist's former name, since the study id still uses it.
top_fixes_with_text: TITLE AND SUBTITLE. Replace with: title: "uniichat through claude code: the mechanics hold, and compaction is the bill" / subtitle: "victor taelin's one-chat-that-never-ends, rebuilt from the october 11 gist and run on haiku, sonnet and opus. one short chat, 1,343 requests, four questions for the author."
